# SK3531 — The `DisposeAsync` override never calls the base implementation

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

An `override` of `DisposeAsync` or `DisposeAsyncCore` never reaches the implementation it replaced, so the base type's asynchronous cleanup stops happening.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Lifetime |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | 8.0 |
| Since | 1.3 |

## Why

Asynchronous disposal is a chain: `DisposeAsync` calls a virtual `DisposeAsyncCore`, and each override finishes by calling the one it overrode. An override that skips the base breaks the chain at that link — the base type's final flush, its graceful close, its return to a pool simply stop running. Nothing says so. There is no compiler diagnostic, no test that fails, and the type still satisfies `IAsyncDisposable`; the resource is released when the process ends, or not at all. `CA1063` pins the synchronous pattern and `CA2215` pins the synchronous base call, and neither has an asynchronous counterpart.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
sealed class Buffered : Writer {
    protected override async ValueTask DisposeAsyncCore() {
        await queue.DrainAsync();
    }
}
```

Write:

```csharp
sealed class Buffered : Writer {
    protected override async ValueTask DisposeAsyncCore() {
        await queue.DrainAsync();
        await base.DisposeAsyncCore();
    }
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **Every finding is provable, and the guards are what makes that true rather than likely.** The overridden method must be declared in *this* compilation and its body must contain at least one invocation. A base in another assembly is a body the rule never reads, and a base whose body is `ValueTask.CompletedTask`, `default` or an empty block loses nothing by being skipped; both withdraw. ⚠ **The cost is a stated gap rather than a hidden one**: a type deriving from a framework base with a real `DisposeAsyncCore` is exactly the case this rule does not cover, and widening it would mean reporting on code the rule cannot see. ⚠ An abstract base has no implementation to lose and is not reported. ⚠ **Any `base.` call at all withdraws it**, not only a call to this method: an override reaching the base type through a different member is participating in the chain in a way the rule has no business second-guessing. ⚠ An override whose entire body is a `throw` is refusing the operation, not forgetting the base. Only the non-generic `ValueTask` and `Task` shapes are matched, and the containing type must implement `IAsyncDisposable`. ⚠ **No fix, and that is a decision.** The call goes last in an override and first in a wrapper, it must be awaited in some bodies and returned in others, and where it belongs among the override's own cleanup is an ordering decision that no edit can read off the text.
